title: Reading literature and poetry
objectives: I can read short literary excerpts by Gonçalves Dias, Machado de Assis, Castro Alves and Álvares de Azevedo and follow their meaning.
I can recognize and name figures of speech such as metaphor, simile, irony, personification and hyperbole.
I can recognize literary forms such as the simple pluperfect, mesoclisis and inverted word order.
I can use context, word families, prefixes and suffixes to work out unfamiliar words, and interpret diminutives and augmentatives.

example.pt: O poeta escreveu esses versos durante o exílio.
example.en: The poet wrote these verses during his exile.

vocabulary.note: A word with no exact English equivalent; it combines missing someone or something with warm nostalgia.

example.pt: A saudade da terra natal acompanhava o poeta.
example.en: Longing for his homeland accompanied the poet.

vocabulary.note: Literary verb for the singing of birds.

example.pt: Os pássaros gorjeiam ao amanhecer.
example.en: The birds warble at dawn.

example.pt: As várzeas ficam verdes depois da chuva.
example.en: The lowland meadows turn green after the rain.

example.pt: Passeamos no bosque ao fim da tarde.
example.en: We strolled in the grove at the end of the afternoon.

vocabulary.note: Literary verb for thinking deeply and often sadly. Em cismar means 'while musing'.

example.pt: Ele passava as noites a cismar à janela.
example.en: He spent his nights brooding at the window.

vocabulary.en: a thing of excellence, a refinement

example.pt: O bordado era um primor de delicadeza.
example.en: The embroidery was a masterpiece of delicacy.

vocabulary.note: A beloved songbird; the sabiá-laranjeira is Brazil's national bird.

example.pt: O sabiá canta na mangueira do quintal.
example.en: The thrush sings in the mango tree in the yard.

example.pt: Uma palmeira alta cobria a casa de sombra.
example.en: A tall palm tree covered the house in shade.

example.pt: O pendão verde e amarelo balançava ao vento.
example.en: The green and yellow banner swayed in the wind.

vocabulary.note: Irregular: eu roo, ele rói, ele roeu.

example.pt: O rato roeu a roupa do rei de Roma.
example.en: The mouse gnawed the clothes of the king of Rome.

vocabulary.note: Literary word; in everyday speech people say túmulo.

example.pt: Deixaram flores sobre a campa do poeta.
example.en: They left flowers on the poet's grave.

vocabulary.note: Figuratively, the place of origin: o berço da cultura.

example.pt: Aquela cidade foi o berço do samba.
example.en: That city was the cradle of samba.

example.pt: O narrador do romance é um defunto que conta a própria vida.
example.en: The narrator of the novel is a dead man who tells his own life.

example.pt: Ela hesitou antes de abrir a carta.
example.en: She hesitated before opening the letter.

example.pt: Uma lágrima escorreu pelo rosto dela.
example.en: A tear ran down her face.

example.pt: O cansaço pesava sobre as pálpebras.
example.en: Tiredness weighed on his eyelids.

example.pt: O último verso do poema é o mais famoso.
example.en: The last line of the poem is the most famous.

example.pt: Cada estrofe desse poema tem quatro versos.
example.en: Each stanza of this poem has four lines.

example.pt: A rima entre céu e véu é muito comum.
example.en: The rhyme between céu and véu is very common.

vocabulary.note: The voice that speaks in a poem, not necessarily the poet himself.

example.pt: O eu lírico sente saudade da pátria.
example.en: The lyrical speaker misses the homeland.

example.pt: Dizer que a vida é um rio é uma metáfora.
example.en: Saying that life is a river is a metaphor.

vocabulary.note: In literary analysis, a comparison uses a word like como or tal qual.

example.pt: Na comparação, o amor é como uma chama.
example.en: In the simile, love is like a flame.

example.pt: A personificação dá vida ao vento no poema.
example.en: Personification gives life to the wind in the poem.

example.pt: Dizer que esperou mil anos é uma hipérbole.
example.en: Saying that one waited a thousand years is a hyperbole.

example.pt: A ironia de Machado de Assis é sempre elegante.
example.en: Machado de Assis's irony is always elegant.

dialogues.title: Aula sobre a Canção do exílio
dialogues.context: In a literature class, Professor Marta and two students discuss the poem Canção do exílio by Gonçalves Dias.

lines.speaker: Marta
lines.pt: Hoje vamos ler a Canção do exílio, de Gonçalves Dias. Alguém sabe quando ela foi escrita?
lines.en: Today we will read the Canção do exílio by Gonçalves Dias. Does anyone know when it was written?

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Em mil oitocentos e quarenta e três, professora. O poeta estava em Portugal, longe do Brasil.
lines.en: In 1843, professor. The poet was in Portugal, far from Brazil.

lines.speaker: Marta
lines.pt: Isso mesmo. E o que o poema revela sobre o sentimento dele?
lines.en: Exactly. And what does the poem reveal about his feelings?

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.pt: Muita saudade. Ele compara a terra dele com o lugar onde está e diz que lá tudo é melhor.
lines.en: A lot of longing. He compares his land with the place where he is and says that everything there is better.

lines.speaker: Marta
lines.pt: Muito bem. Reparem que ele não diz o nome do país. Fala só de palmeiras e do sabiá.
lines.en: Very good. Notice that he does not say the name of the country. He speaks only of palm trees and the thrush.

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Então as palmeiras e o sabiá são símbolos da pátria?
lines.en: So the palm trees and the thrush are symbols of the homeland?

lines.speaker: Marta
lines.pt: Exatamente. Reparem também nos versos curtos e no ritmo, que lembram uma canção.
lines.en: Exactly. Notice also the short lines and the rhythm, which remind us of a song.

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.pt: No fim ele pede a Deus que não o deixe morrer sem voltar para lá.
lines.en: At the end he asks God not to let him die without going back there.

lines.speaker: Marta
lines.pt: Sim, e nesse momento o tom muda. Da comparação alegre passamos ao desejo profundo de voltar.
lines.en: Yes, and at that moment the tone changes. From the cheerful comparison we move to the deep wish to return.

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Dá para ver por que tanta gente ainda cita esse poema.
lines.en: You can see why so many people still quote this poem.

dialogues.title: Clube do livro
dialogues.context: Three friends at a book club discuss Machado de Assis, the master of irony in Brazilian literature.

lines.speaker: Rita
lines.pt: Terminei Memórias Póstumas de Brás Cubas. O narrador já começa dizendo que é um defunto autor!
lines.en: I finished Memórias Póstumas de Brás Cubas. The narrator starts right away by saying he is a dead author!

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.pt: É o que mais me diverte. Ele conta a própria vida depois de morto e ainda faz piada com isso.
lines.en: That is what amuses me most. He tells his own life after dying and even jokes about it.

lines.speaker: Zélia
lines.pt: Isso é ironia pura. Machado nunca diz as coisas diretamente. Ele deixa o leitor concluir.
lines.en: That is pure irony. Machado never says things directly. He lets the reader conclude.

lines.speaker: Rita
lines.pt: Verdade. Na dedicatória, ele oferece o livro ao verme que roeu as frias carnes do cadáver.
lines.en: True. In the dedication, he offers the book to the worm that gnawed the cold flesh of his corpse.

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.pt: Eu ri alto. É macabro, mas é engraçado. Era muito ousado para a época.
lines.en: I laughed out loud. It is macabre, but funny. It was very daring for its time.

lines.speaker: Zélia
lines.pt: Já em Dom Casmurro o tom muda. O narrador parece simpático, mas a gente começa a desconfiar dele.
lines.en: In Dom Casmurro the tone changes. The narrator seems likable, but we start to distrust him.

lines.speaker: Rita
lines.pt: Será que a Capitu traiu mesmo o Bentinho? Até hoje os leitores discutem isso.
lines.en: Did Capitu really betray Bentinho? To this day readers argue about it.

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.pt: Eu acho que não. Ele tinha ciúme de tudo, e talvez tudo fosse imaginação dele.
lines.en: I think not. He was jealous of everything, and perhaps everything was his imagination.

lines.speaker: Zélia
lines.pt: Essa é a graça. Machado escreveu o livro de modo que ninguém chegasse a uma certeza.
lines.en: That is the beauty of it. Machado wrote the book so that nobody could reach certainty.

lines.speaker: Rita
lines.pt: Vou reler com outros olhos. Me empresta a sua edição, Caio?
lines.en: I will reread it with new eyes. Will you lend me your edition, Caio?

dialogues.title: Oficina de escrita
dialogues.context: Carla shows a short story about her grandmother's house to her friend Paulo, who asks about her many diminutives.

lines.speaker: Carla
lines.pt: Paulo, escrevi um conto sobre a casa da minha avó. Quer ler?
lines.en: Paulo, I wrote a short story about my grandmother's house. Do you want to read it?

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Claro! Mas por que você usa tantos diminutivos? Casinha, ruazinha, fogãozinho.
lines.en: Sure! But why do you use so many diminutives? Casinha, ruazinha, fogãozinho.

lines.speaker: Carla
lines.pt: É de propósito. O diminutivo mostra carinho, não apenas tamanho.
lines.en: It is on purpose. The diminutive shows affection, not just size.

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Entendi. E o cachorrão do quintal? Esse já é o contrário.
lines.en: I see. And the big dog in the yard? That is the opposite.

lines.speaker: Carla
lines.pt: Isso. O aumentativo dá ideia de algo grande, mas aqui também é afetuoso. Ele era enorme e preguiçoso.
lines.en: Right. The augmentative suggests something big, but here it is affectionate too. He was huge and lazy.

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Deu vontade de comer pão de queijo com um cafezinho.
lines.en: It made me want to eat cheese bread with a little coffee.

lines.speaker: Carla
lines.pt: É o efeito que eu queria! Tem uma frase de que eu gosto muito: a saudade, essa sim, continuava enorme.
lines.en: That is the effect I wanted! There is a sentence I like a lot: the longing, that one yes, remained enormous.

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Essa frase ficou ótima. Dá para sentir que você escreveu com o coração.
lines.en: That sentence turned out great. You can feel you wrote it with your heart.

lines.speaker: Carla
lines.pt: Obrigada. Vou mandar o texto para um concurso de contos.
lines.en: Thank you. I am going to send the text to a short story contest.

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Boa sorte! E não esquece de me dedicar o livro quando ficar famosa.
lines.en: Good luck! And don't forget to dedicate the book to me when you become famous.

grammar.title: Literary tenses and word order
grammar.explanation:
Literary Portuguese keeps forms that have almost disappeared from speech. The most common is the simple pluperfect, formed from the third person plural of the preterite by replacing -ram with -ra, -ras, -ra, -ramos, -reis, -ram: falara, comera, partira. It means the same as the compound pluperfect (tinha falado): Ele disse que já chegara means he said he had already arrived. Irregular verbs follow the same pattern: dissera, fizera, vira, viera, tivera. The form fora (from ser and ir) is especially frequent: o pedido fora registrado, fora para casa.

The word order of literary prose is freer than in speech. The verb may come before the subject (Disse o poeta...), adjectives may come before the noun for emphasis (as frias carnes), and the object pronoun follows the verb (cumprimentou-me, sentou-se), including mesoclisis in the future and conditional (dar-lhe-ia, far-se-á). Subjects are often omitted.

These forms create a formal, elevated tone. Learn to recognize them when reading; in your own writing, use them sparingly and only when the register calls for it.

examples.pt: Ele disse que já chegara ao porto.
examples.en: He said he had already reached the port.

examples.pt: Cumprimentou-me, sentou-se ao pé de mim e falou da lua.
examples.en: He greeted me, sat down next to me and spoke of the moon.

examples.pt: Nunca vira tanta beleza numa só noite.
examples.en: He had never seen so much beauty in a single night.

examples.pt: As frias carnes do cadáver foram roídas pelo verme.
examples.en: The cold flesh of the corpse was gnawed by the worm.

examples.pt: Dir-se-ia que o rio chorava.
examples.en: One would say that the river was crying.

grammar.title: Figures of speech
grammar.explanation:
A figure of speech (figura de linguagem) uses words in a non-literal way to create an effect. Recognizing the common ones helps you understand what a poet or novelist really means.

A metáfora identifies one thing with another without a linking word: meu coração é um barco. A comparação makes the likeness explicit with como, tal qual or feito: forte como um touro. Personificação gives human actions to an object, animal or idea: o vento conta segredos. Hipérbole deliberately exaggerates: esperei mil anos. Ironia says the opposite of what is meant, or lets the reader see the gap between words and truth: Que ótimo, choveu no dia do piquenique! Machado de Assis is famous for refined irony.

When you read a poem, ask three questions: which two things are being connected, what feeling does the connection create, and would the literal statement have the same effect. The answer to the third is almost always no. That difference is the poetry.

examples.pt: Meu coração é um barco sem remo e sem bandeira.
examples.en: My heart is a boat without an oar and without a flag.

examples.pt: Ele era forte como um touro.
examples.en: He was as strong as a bull.

examples.pt: A tarde, vestida de ouro, deita-se sobre o rio.
examples.en: The afternoon, dressed in gold, lies down on the river.

examples.pt: Esperei mil anos e o mar não teve tanta água quanta lágrima deixei.
examples.en: I waited a thousand years and the sea did not have as much water as the tears I left.

examples.pt: Que simpático: ele me acordou às cinco da manhã para pedir um favor.
examples.en: How nice of him: he woke me at five in the morning to ask a favor.

grammar.title: Reading strategies: context, word families, prefixes and suffixes
grammar.explanation:
You do not need a dictionary for every unknown word in a literary text. Start with context: the words around an unfamiliar term, the part of speech it must be, and the tone of the passage often reveal its meaning. In Os pássaros gorjeiam no bosque, you can guess that gorjeiam is something birds do.

Next, look for word families. Terra gives terreno, enterrar, terrestre, aterrissar. Água gives aguaceiro, aquático, desaguar. Knowing a root makes a whole family readable.

Finally, break the word into prefix, root and suffix. Common prefixes: in- or im- (not: inútil, impossível), des- (reversal: desfazer), re- (again: reler), pré- (before: pré-história), sub- (under: subterrâneo). Common suffixes: -mente (adverb: lentamente), -ção (noun from a verb: criação), -eiro (person or tree: padeiro, mangueira), -ável or -ível (can be done: amável, possível), -oso (full of: saudoso, perigoso). Learning twenty prefixes and suffixes can unlock hundreds of words.

examples.pt: Saudoso é quem sente saudade.
examples.en: Saudoso describes someone who feels saudade.

examples.pt: O desespero é o contrário da esperança.
examples.en: Despair is the opposite of hope.

examples.pt: Ela releu a carta três vezes antes de responder.
examples.en: She reread the letter three times before answering.

examples.pt: Da palavra terra vêm terreno, enterrar e terrestre.
examples.en: From the word terra come terreno, enterrar and terrestre.

examples.pt: A sala estava silenciosa, quase inabitável.
examples.en: The room was silent, almost uninhabitable.

grammar.title: Diminutives and augmentatives
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese adds -inho or -zinho to make a diminutive, and -ão, -zão or -ona to make an augmentative. The meaning is not only size. A diminutive often expresses affection (casinha, amorzinho), politeness or softening (um cafezinho, um probleminha), while an augmentative can mean large (casarão) or express admiration or scorn (um medrosão, uma mulherona).

Formation: words ending in an unstressed vowel drop it before -inho (casa gives casinha, livro gives livrinho). Words ending in a stressed vowel, a nasal or a consonant add -zinho (café gives cafezinho, pão gives pãozinho, flor gives florzinha, mulher gives mulherzinha). In the plural, -zinho is pluralized at both ends in careful writing (pãezinhos). The feminine augmentative often ends in -ona (mesa gives mesona), the masculine in -ão (cachorro gives cachorrão).

Brazilians use diminutives much more than English speakers. A moment can be um minutinho, a coffee um cafezinho, a price um precinho. In literary texts, diminutives build tenderness and memory. Translate the feeling, not the size.

examples.pt: Aceita um cafezinho?
examples.en: Would you like a little coffee?

examples.pt: A casinha da vovó ficava no fim da rua.
examples.en: Grandmother's little house was at the end of the street.

examples.pt: O cachorrão dormia o dia inteiro no quintal.
examples.en: The big dog slept all day in the yard.

examples.pt: Tenho só um probleminha para resolver.
examples.en: I only have a little problem to solve.

examples.pt: Ela virou uma mulherona e mudou de cidade.
examples.en: She became a strong, grown woman and moved to another city.

culture.title: Quatro vozes da literatura brasileira
culture.text:
Brazilian literature has its roots in the nineteenth century, when the young nation looked for its own voice. Gonçalves Dias (1823 to 1864) wrote the Canção do exílio in 1843 while studying in Portugal. Its first lines are so well known that Brazilians have parodied them for generations, and the national anthem itself echoes its images of stars, flowers and groves. Gonçalves Dias died in a shipwreck returning to Brazil.

Castro Alves (1847 to 1871), known as the Poet of the Slaves, used grand, dramatic verse to denounce slavery, in poems such as Navio Negreiro. Álvares de Azevedo (1831 to 1852) died at twenty and became the emblem of dark, melancholic Romantic poetry, with themes of death, solitude and lost love.

Machado de Assis (1839 to 1908) was born in Rio de Janeiro to a poor family and became the greatest Brazilian novelist. He was the first president of the Academia Brasileira de Letras, founded in 1897. His narrators, such as Brás Cubas and Bentinho, are witty and unreliable, and his irony still surprises readers today. All four authors are in the public domain in Brazil, so their works can be read and shared freely. Reading them is the best way to meet a formal, beautiful Portuguese that is far from everyday speech but still shapes how Brazilians think about language and identity.

readings.title: Canção do exílio, de Gonçalves Dias

paragraphs.pt: Minha terra tem palmeiras, onde canta o Sabiá; as aves, que aqui gorjeiam, não gorjeiam como lá.
paragraphs.en: My land has palm trees where the thrush sings; the birds that warble here do not warble like there.

paragraphs.pt: Nosso céu tem mais estrelas, nossas várzeas têm mais flores, nossos bosques têm mais vida, nossa vida mais amores.
paragraphs.en: Our sky has more stars, our meadows have more flowers, our groves have more life, our life has more love.

paragraphs.pt: Não permita Deus que eu morra, sem que eu volte para lá; sem que desfrute os primores que não encontro por cá; sem que ainda aviste as palmeiras, onde canta o Sabiá.
paragraphs.en: May God not allow me to die without my returning there; without my enjoying the fine things that I do not find here; without my still seeing the palm trees where the thrush sings. The original elides que ainda into qu'inda.

questions.prompt: Where is the lyrical speaker in the poem?
choices: In his homeland, among the palm trees
Far from his homeland, missing it
questions.explanation: The words aqui and lá, and the last stanza, show he is away and wants to return.

questions.prompt: What do the palm trees and the thrush represent?
choices: His home country, through symbols of its nature
A new country he wants to visit
questions.explanation: The poet never names the country; he evokes it with nature symbols.

questions.prompt: What is the central wish expressed in the last stanza?
choices: To never leave his homeland again
To travel to a new place
To see his homeland again before dying
questions.explanation: He asks that he not die without going back and seeing the palm trees.

questions.prompt: In the second stanza the poet says nossa vida mais amores. What effect is created?
choices: A hyperbole celebrating his homeland as richer in everything
questions.explanation: Repetition and the claim that everything is more abundant at home express longing and idealization.

readings.title: Duas aberturas de Machado de Assis

paragraphs.pt: Ao verme que primeiro roeu as frias carnes do meu cadáver dedico como saudosa lembrança estas Memórias Póstumas.
paragraphs.en: To the worm that first gnawed the cold flesh of my corpse I dedicate these Posthumous Memoirs as a fond remembrance. From Memórias Póstumas de Brás Cubas.

paragraphs.pt: Algum tempo hesitei se devia abrir estas memórias pelo princípio ou pelo fim, isto é, se poria em primeiro lugar o meu nascimento ou a minha morte.
paragraphs.en: For some time I hesitated whether I should open these memoirs at the beginning or at the end, that is, whether I should put my birth or my death first.

paragraphs.pt: Suposto o uso vulgar seja começar pelo nascimento, duas considerações me levaram a adotar diferente método:
paragraphs.en: Although common usage is to begin with birth, two considerations led me to adopt a different method:

paragraphs.pt: a primeira é que eu não sou propriamente um autor defunto, mas um defunto autor, para quem a campa foi outro berço;
paragraphs.en: the first is that I am not properly a dead author but an author who is dead, for whom the grave was another cradle;

paragraphs.pt: a segunda é que o escrito ficaria assim mais galante e mais novo.
paragraphs.en: the second is that the writing would thus be more elegant and newer.

paragraphs.pt: Uma noite destas, vindo da cidade para o Engenho Novo, encontrei num trem da Central um rapaz aqui do bairro, que eu conheço de vista e de chapéu.
paragraphs.en: One of these nights, coming from the city to Engenho Novo, I met on a Central train a young man from the neighborhood, whom I know by sight and by hat.

paragraphs.pt: Cumprimentou-me, sentou-se ao pé de mim, falou da lua e dos ministros, e acabou recitando-me versos.
paragraphs.en: He greeted me, sat down next to me, spoke of the moon and the ministers, and ended up reciting verses to me. From Dom Casmurro.

questions.prompt: To whom does Brás Cubas dedicate his memoirs?
choices: The worm that gnawed his corpse
questions.explanation: The ironic dedication is ao verme que primeiro roeu as frias carnes do meu cadáver.

questions.prompt: What does Brás Cubas say he hesitated about?
choices: Whether to begin with his birth or his death
Whether to use his real name
questions.explanation: He hesitates between opening pelo princípio ou pelo fim.

questions.prompt: What is the humor in defunto autor rather than autor defunto?
choices: He was a dead man who became an author after death
He is an author who is pretending to be dead
He is an author who writes about funerals
He is a dead author of old books
questions.explanation: The joke turns on word order: the narrator is a dead man writing, not a writer who happened to die.

questions.prompt: Where does the second passage take place?
questions.explanation: The narrator meets a young man num trem da Central.

readings.title: Castro Alves e Álvares de Azevedo

paragraphs.pt: Auriverde pendão de minha terra, que a brisa do Brasil beija e balança, estandarte que a luz do sol encerra e as promessas divinas da esperança.
paragraphs.en: Green and gold banner of my land, which the Brazilian breeze kisses and sways, standard that holds the light of the sun and the divine promises of hope. From Castro Alves, Navio Negreiro.

paragraphs.pt: Se eu morresse amanhã, viria ao menos fechar meus olhos minha triste irmã; minha mãe de saudades morreria se eu morresse amanhã!
paragraphs.en: If I died tomorrow, at least my sad sister would come to close my eyes; my mother would die of longing if I died tomorrow! From Álvares de Azevedo.

questions.prompt: What figure of speech is a brisa do Brasil beija e balança o pendão?
questions.explanation: The breeze is given a human action, kissing.

questions.prompt: What is the tone of the Álvares de Azevedo lines?
questions.explanation: The thought of dying and the sister and mother who would grieve give a melancholic tone.

questions.prompt: What grammatical pattern is used in Se eu morresse amanhã, viria ao menos...?
questions.explanation: Morresse is the imperfect subjunctive and viria is the conditional, used for an unreal hypothesis.

readings.title: Dois textos originais no estilo literário, escritos para este curso

paragraphs.pt: O vento conta segredos às folhas da mangueira. A tarde, vestida de ouro, deita-se sobre o rio.
paragraphs.en: The wind tells secrets to the leaves of the mango tree. The afternoon, dressed in gold, lies down on the river.

paragraphs.pt: Meu coração é um barco sem remo e sem bandeira, que a saudade empurra nas noites de frio.
paragraphs.en: My heart is a boat without an oar and without a flag, which longing pushes on cold nights.

paragraphs.pt: Esperei mil anos, e o mar não teve tanta água quanta lágrima deixei na soleira da porta.
paragraphs.en: I waited a thousand years, and the sea did not have as much water as the tears I left on the doorstep.

paragraphs.pt: A casinha da vovó ficava no fim de uma ruazinha de terra, entre um cafezal velho e um riozinho que cantava o ano inteiro.
paragraphs.en: Grandmother's little house stood at the end of a little dirt street, between an old coffee plantation and a little river that sang all year.

paragraphs.pt: Lá dentro havia uma mesona de madeira, onde cabiam todos os primos, e um fogãozinho a lenha que nunca se apagava.
paragraphs.en: Inside there was a big wooden table where all the cousins fit, and a little wood stove that never went out.

paragraphs.pt: Quando cresci, voltei lá e encontrei a casa menor do que me lembrava. Mas o cheirinho de pão de queijo era o mesmo, e a saudade, essa sim, continuava enorme.
paragraphs.en: When I grew up, I went back and found the house smaller than I remembered. But the little smell of cheese bread was the same, and the longing, that one yes, remained enormous.

questions.prompt: Which line of the original poem is a metaphor?
